talks.title: AI for Impact
talks.summary: Keynoted the Philadelphia Eagles' 12th annual Eagles Care Summit at Lincoln Financial Field on March 18, 2026, delivering "AI for Impact" to more than 300 community and business leaders.
talks.lead: I showed nonprofit leaders how to put AI to work for their missions, starting with the basics of models and prompts and building up to Claude skills, agents and retrieval over their own documents.
talks.context: The summit is the team’s yearly gathering of Philadelphia’s nonprofit community, and this year’s room came from more than 150 local nonprofits. Praxtera’s live two-hour session was built around AI they could use right away.
talks.course: From Praxtera’s AI Basics - Prompting course, with the higher-level concepts of its AI Agents - RAG, Workflows, Skills, and More course.

parts.title: How the models work
paras: The session opened on one question for the room, “How are you using AI today?” Attendees traded what they already use it for and their time-saving shortcuts.
A model is like a student made to read most of the internet: it learns patterns without understanding them and predicts one word at a time. That is why it can miss nuance or invent facts.

parts.title: Choosing the right model
paras: Most work needs one generalist, such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot. Know when to call a specialist: Perplexity when an answer needs citations, Claude for very long reports, Copilot inside Word, Excel and Outlook, NotebookLM for your own files.

parts.title: Writing better prompts
paras: A prompt works like a brief to a very literal assistant. H4W covers who you are, what you need, why, who it is for and how it should look; COSTAR adds context, objective, style, tone, audience and response.

parts.title: AI across your workflows
paras: Then where AI fits in a working day: a long report turned into a few key points, a hard email started from a first draft instead of a blank page, and messy meeting notes turned into action items.

parts.title: Claude skills
paras: Claude skills were still very new. A skill saves the instructions for one kind of task so Claude can reuse them, the same idea as a custom GPT in ChatGPT, an agent in Copilot or a Gem in Gemini.

parts.title: Skills, MCPs, plugins, workflows and agents
paras: How the pieces differ: a skill holds the know-how for a task, an MCP server connects the model to outside tools and data, and a plugin packages these to install in one step.
A workflow runs the same steps every time; an agent works toward a goal and chooses its own steps, including which workflow to call.

parts.title: Retrieval over your own documents
paras: Retrieval-augmented generation lets the model look things up in an organization’s documents first. It finds the passages that matter, adds them to the prompt and answers from them, so its answers rest on that organization’s information.

quote.text: Praxtera doesn’t just teach AI, they make it usable. More than 300 leaders walked away not just understanding AI, but actively applying it in their daily work. That’s the difference between exposure and real adoption.
quote.by: Tina D’Orazio, Chief of Staff, Philadelphia Eagles

parts.title: AI Basics: Prompting
parts.heading: First session
parts.course: Built on Praxtera’s AI Basics - Prompting course.
paras: Generative AI explained plainly: a language model is not magic; it predicts the most likely answer from patterns it has learned. Most people can stick with one tool, such as Copilot, and call on a specialist for the rest.

Prompting practice used their own customers: a vague delay email for a clinic waiting on Phonak devices, rewritten using H4W and COSTAR, then a reply to a hearing care professional, refined until it was ready to send.

I ran the demo on Sonova’s own published reports: an outline for a briefing for new US employees, a performance section citing the file and page for every number, then a deck and an email to share it.
Then one Phonak EON paragraph, rewritten for a first-time hearing aid wearer, an audiologist and a worried adult daughter, with one check: did the model add any claim or number the source never made?

parts.title: AI Agents: RAG, Workflows, Skills, and More
parts.heading: Second session
parts.displayTitle: Save It Once, Check It Every Time
parts.course: Built on Praxtera’s AI Agents - RAG, Workflows, Skills, and More course.
paras: A Project is the room where files and instructions wait; a skill is a recipe you carry into any room. In a Project, Claude explained a repair center’s overtime from the notes; a chat with no files guessed.

Grounding works like an open-book exam: the model finds the passages that match, sets them beside the request, and answers from them. Hand it an outdated file and you get a confident, outdated answer.

Participants built one skill on September’s made-up budget-versus-actual export, then ran it on October’s with one line. Same model, same file: a plain chat guessed at causes, while the skill wrote “Needs explanation”.

The checks, in Excel: is each variance a formula, does the overtime flag hold when redone by hand, what happened to a freight line with no budget, and did the skill give any reason the file never did?
One fix went into the rules on the spot: mark a row with no budget as “No budget” instead of calculating a percent, then rebuild and rerun October.
Each person then built a skill for a task they repeat, from their survey answers: a KPI scorecard, WIP aging or a weekly Teams update, tested on made-up data until IT approves a tool.

engagements.lead: I taught a regional PBS station’s team how generative AI works, what has to be settled before anyone uses it, and how to turn work that pulls staff from the mission into workflows and simple agents.
engagements.context: The room was one regional PBS member station: newsroom, programming, membership and grant staff, working across TV, radio and Microsoft 365. Every example in the session was rebuilt around public media work.
engagements.credit: I led the AI content as subject-matter expert, alongside Michelle Histand, communications strategist and nonprofit leader.

parts.title: AI foundations
parts.text: What generative AI is and isn’t, how large language models work, and where they fail.
paras: Generative AI, in three words: advanced Google search. Search is already a prediction engine, and a large language model is a far more powerful version of that prediction, one word at a time.

A custom GPT is an app running on the model as its operating system. Retrieval-augmented generation sits under the hood: it lays the organization’s own files over the model, so answers come from that material.

Tool choice came from a programming director’s real task: ChatGPT to turn ratings, streaming and social data into one performance story, Claude to mine viewer feedback for underserved audiences, and Perplexity to benchmark reach against other public media.

parts.title: Data privacy and governance first
parts.text: Privacy and governance frameworks as the first step, and how they set what AI can safely be used for.

parts.title: First steps toward AI ROI
paras: A workflow runs predefined steps the same way every time. An agent reasons, plans and decides which workflows to use toward a goal.

Examples were set in the station’s work, in Copilot: a daily rundown drafted from recent email and the calendar, one script rewritten for radio, web, social and the member newsletter, and a grant narrative built from stored impact reports.
steps: Start with the pain points that take employees’ time away from work central to the mission.
Break each pain point into a list of steps.
Run those steps with a deterministic script, workflow, or skill.
When the automations need coordinating, add simple agents, and let the coordination grow more complex rather than the agents themselves.
Keep each agent simple enough to audit, and put the complexity in the relationships between agents.

parts.title: From resistance to persuasion
parts.text: Participants listed why partners, associates, and staff would refuse AI. Gemini sorted that board into ten resister personas, from the accuracy skeptic to the billable-hour traditionalist. In a live roleplay, Gemini played one persona while I used the CLEAR framework to win them over. Groups then wrote persuasion messages for their own persona and designed a champion’s toolkit: a green, yellow, and red guide to which tasks are safe for AI, office hours, flash cards, and prompt-off competitions.

parts.course: Taught at HP as Applying AI in IT and Digital Solutions, built on Praxtera’s AI Agents - RAG, Workflows, Skills, and More course.
parts.text: Retrieval-augmented generation, vector databases, and knowledge graphs; custom GPTs; the difference between AI workflows and agents, and a checklist for when an agent is worth building; and AI governance. paras: Retrieval was shown on their own work: a store of sample business and functional requirements sits in front of the model, so it translates a new RFP from the team’s own documents.

A workflow follows fixed steps; an agent reasons and picks which workflows to run. The AGENT checklist: autonomous, goal-oriented, error-tolerant, necessary info, time saving. Strategic decisions, one-time tasks and judgment calls stay with people.
The troubleshooter followed a live agent build: it greets the user, identifies the issue, walks through fixes or hands off to a person, and confirms the resolution.

parts.title: Prompt engineering
paras: Why structure and context change what a model writes. The team rewrote vague prompts with the 5 W’s + How and COSTAR frameworks, and wrote image prompts with VISUAL.
Then one piece of bad news, a delayed software rollout, went to four audiences: a colleague, the CEO, customers and an all-hands. Same facts, four messages.
Everyday patterns followed: a 15-message email thread summarized into decisions, owners and deadlines; a budget request built on AIDA; and one board summary drawn from five department reports.

parts.title: Which model for which task
paras: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot and NotebookLM side by side. One generalist covers most work; each also has a specialty, such as Perplexity for cited research, Claude for long documents and Copilot inside Microsoft 365.

parts.title: Trust, but verify
paras: How models learn patterns from examples, and why that makes them miss nuance, amplify bias and state made-up facts with confidence, shown with a live hallucination example. The rule: always verify, always edit.

parts.title: Personas and roleplay

talks.title: Knowledge Graphs, Then Small Language Models
talks.summary: Presented what a knowledge graph is, how it enriches questions before they reach a model, and how it checks the model’s answer afterward, then where graphs go next: sub-graphs by topic, failure graphs, codified expertise, and the graph behind an API. Covered small language models next: what they are, when to go small and when to go big, a live setup of a local model in five minutes, and how they change the way people work.
talks.context: Atos is a global, AI-powered technology partner. This was an independent talk, and each graph example ran twice: once for a hospital or a bank, once for IT operations.

sessions.displayTitle: Plan Big, Run Small, Check with the Graph

parts.title: Nouns, verbs, adjectives
paras: A node is a noun, an edge is a verb and a property is an adjective. Models draft the graph, people verify it, and only verified edges are the authority.
The same shape relabels in place, from a patient, her doctor and her drugs to a client, its payment service, the server it runs on, a change and an incident.

parts.title: Before the model, and after
paras: Before the model, the graph finds the facts that matter and a verified example of a good answer. Asked if a patient with a penicillin allergy can take amoxicillin, the model gave a safe no.
For a failing payment service, the same path led through its server to a library upgrade seventeen minutes before the incident, and to a rollback.
After the model, an agent’s answer becomes a chain of claims tested against the graph. Blaming the data centre failed and went back as feedback; naming the change passed.
The graph is only an authority while someone keeps it current.

parts.title: Small models fit in the room
paras: A small model runs on one laptop or one GPU, usually under fifteen billion parameters. It keeps data in the building, but reasons less well and needs sharper prompts, evaluation and often fine-tuning.

Four sliders set the choice: how sensitive the data is, how many requests, how hard the thinking and how fast the answer. Hard thinking on secret data meant the largest open model your hardware allows.
Then the setup, in three commands: install Ollama, run Gemma 4 12B, and call the same model as an API on the laptop.

parts.title: Big model plans, small models execute, graph checks
paras: A small model does not want a conversation; it wants a task. A vague question about a payment problem got a generic answer. A narrow task with the graph’s facts named the change and the rollback.
Together: a frontier model breaks the request into narrow tasks, small models run each one on your hardware, and the graph checks every claim.

research.title: Drone-Megaddon
research.subtitle: A Real-Time Strategy Interface for Managing Drone Swarms
research.summary: I co-built an end-to-end Android, radio, and embedded-control prototype that translated real-time strategy interactions into drone commands. The 2014 work established the command interface and execution path; Drone-Megaddon 2026 extends that foundation with a proposed language-and-vision architecture for operator-supervised coordination.

research.title: Drone-Megaddon 2026
research.subtitle: Co-Intelligent Swarm Control with Language and Vision Models
research.summary: I coauthored a proposed extension of our built 2014 drone-control prototype: translate operator language into checked commands, ground references in video and track targets, then coordinate assignments across drones. The architecture places language and vision models inside an operator-supervised system, with explicit choices about edge versus cloud execution, latency, bandwidth, and degraded connectivity. An illustrative search-and-rescue trace shows how the layers work together; the paper reports no quantitative results from a deployed 2026 system.

claim.value: Drone-Megaddon 2026: Co-Intelligent Swarm Control with Language and Vision Models

research.title: Who Trains the Next Senior?
research.subtitle: Managing Software Engineering When AI Makes Code Cheap
research.summary: I coauthored a framework for leading engineering organizations when AI makes code abundant but verification and judgment remain scarce. It connects review theater, engineer development, and team incentives to practical changes: smaller reviewable units, scrutiny matched to consequence, evidence-backed gates, and outcome-based metrics. An exploratory, correlational analysis of several thousand commits from a single organization illustrates why raw activity can overstate progress; the paper turns those observations into testable propositions about verification and apprenticeship.

research.title: A Multi-Layer Framework for Evaluating the Return on Investment of AI Projects
research.authors: Sairam Krishnan, Sonia Gandhi, Andrea Hepp
research.summary: I coauthored a decision framework connecting AI strategy to investment and execution: assess organizational readiness, trace business value through ROIC, phase investment through evidence-based gates, and synthesize a decision scorecard. An eight-category risk assessment makes inference economics, vendor dependency, and organizational friction explicit. Eight illustrative public-company cases, from Salesforce and Spotify to JPMorgan and NatWest, show how the framework changes investment conditions across deployment types; this is illustrative validation, not empirical validation. The work was a Wharton independent study sponsored by Professor Gad Allon.

claim.value: A Multi-Layer Framework for Evaluating the ROI of AI Projects

ventures.name: Ondoway
ventures.thesis: A travel companion that adapts as you walk.
ventures.problem: A useful tour must connect accurate stories with personal interests, walking constraints, and the time a traveler actually has.
ventures.role: Co-founder & CTO. I lead technical strategy, AI architecture, and end-to-end engineering within the founding team.
ventures.system: Graph-grounded storytelling, deterministic itinerary planning, GPS-triggered narration, and calibrated LLM judges against frozen human labels. I trace model and prompt versions, evidence, tokens, latency, and costs—including failed attempts.
ventures.state: Private beta with early testers, including Wharton Executive MBA peers, and initial city support for New York City and Paris. Flutter app, FastAPI backend, and Neo4j graph.
ventures.lesson: I rejected a cheaper factual judge after calibration exposed false rejections of legitimate paraphrases, separating model-quality failures from truncation before making the cost decision.

ventures.name: Persuaider
ventures.thesis: Practice, simulate, and evaluate the hard conversation.
ventures.problem: Negotiation practice needs credible competing interests and feedback grounded in what was actually said and agreed.
ventures.role: Creator & AI Engineering Lead. I built the product, agent behavior, multiagent simulation, and evaluation systems.
ventures.system: Role-conditioned agents with private objectives; stateful AI-versus-AI simulations; LLM deal extraction followed by deterministic utility, walk-away, and value-left-on-the-table calculations; configurable weighted coaching rubrics.
ventures.state: Working interactive practice and autonomous simulations with persisted transcripts and usage. Coaching quotations and numerical references are checked in code, returned for bounded repair, and withheld if validation still fails.
ventures.lesson: I evaluate negotiation economics separately from conversational skill, and require the coaching to point back to its evidence.

ventures.name: Gestiq
ventures.thesis: Deliberate desktop actions from hand motion.
ventures.problem: Camera input is uncertain; useful gesture control must distinguish an intentional action from jitter, tracking loss, and return motion.
ventures.role: Creator. I designed and built the native macOS product, extending my CMU hand-controlled 2048 capstone.
ventures.system: On-device Apple Vision hand-pose estimation, palm-normalized temporal recognition, two-hand controls, and application- and website-aware command routing. Latest-frame processing, target revalidation, and live diagnostics connect perception to guarded actions.
ventures.state: Working macOS application with a SwiftUI interface, menu-bar controls, and local camera processing without uploading video.
ventures.lesson: I carry confidence, timing, and target identity through the whole perception-to-action path, including the final dispatch check.

claim.value: Gestiq: on-device computer vision and contextual gesture control

ventures.name: Lore / DependIQ
ventures.thesis: The verification layer AI coding agents lack.
ventures.problem: Repository-local tooling cannot explain the organization-wide blast radius of a dependency change.
ventures.role: Designed the product, graph model, algorithms, and senior-engineer audit.
ventures.system: PostgreSQL for identity and history, Neo4j for dependency traversal, and task-aware model routing across hosted and local models.
ventures.state: Working multi-tenant product with more than 200 tests.
ventures.lesson: AI-assisted engineering needs explicit dependency truth before it needs another generator.

ventures.name: Crucible
ventures.thesis: Engineering workflows that make agents show their work.
ventures.problem: An agent’s confident report is insufficient evidence that a change is correct, complete, or recoverable.
ventures.role: I turn engineering judgment into reusable agent workflows, adversarial review, and executable acceptance rules.
ventures.system: Structured agent reports, claim-level evidence checks, risk-based verification, mutation and undo evidence, concurrent review, and bounded revision loops.
ventures.state: Public toolkit with runtime hooks and regression tests. Separately, my internal agent-engineering work supports daily operations and was adopted and extended by QA, Operations, and upstream/downstream teams.
ventures.lesson: I separate model judgment from the code that checks evidence structure, enforces workflow decisions, and controls when work can proceed.
